description: We are a multidisciplinary Brazilian team from the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG), uniting researchers in Aerospace Engineering and Information Systems. Agriculture drives Brazil's economy and global food security, and we see firsthand how soil degradation threatens farmers' livelihoods. We apply rigorous science to turn NASA Earth observations into practical crop rotation strategies for farmers worldwide.
summary:
Aftercrop helps a farmer decide what follows soybeans on one field, before buying second-crop inputs: keep second-crop corn, add grass to the corn, or test wheat on part of the area. The page answers "Keep what you do", "Try it on a strip here", "Tied" or "Not enough evidence".

Three kinds of evidence sit side by side. NASA HLS shows when this field was green in 8 seasons. NASA POWER summarizes historical cold-night and rainfall exposure across seasons. Embrapa trials from 3 sites show what the next soybean gained. The farmer's prices decide if it pays.

On three real fields in northern Paraná, Brazil, corn with grass gets "Try it on a strip here" at example prices. We tested our crop model against the trials. Label: Model not validated here, so it stays out of the answer. No field trials, no verdict. Aftercrop supports local judgment and does not replace it.
details:
The problem and the user

After the soybean harvest in northern Paraná, farmers ask every year what goes in this field next. In 2016/17, 86% of the soybean area of Londrina and Maringá was followed by second-crop corn (Embrapa Soja, Documentos 398). Frost before maturity limits that corn, wheat is limited to half the area, and the gain in the next soybean comes in some seasons only. The useful question is on which field, and on how much of it, another option is worth a test.

The user is a farmer with the agronomist who advises them. The example farmer is fictional. The fields are real, with no owner data.

What the tool answers on three real fields

The page opens on one of 3 real fields in Cambé, with three columns: Keep corn (the current rotation), Corn with grass (brachiaria added, not simulated) and Wheat on part (up to half of the area). Each has a Why? panel with evidence, gaps and risks for local review.

From the farmer's prices and costs, the page computes the extra bags of soybean per hectare the change needs to pay, and counts the trial site-seasons that reached that gain.

On all three fields, Corn with grass needs 4 extra bags/ha at the base example prices, and trials reached that in 6 of 7 site-seasons: "Try it on a strip here" in all three price scenarios. That is a count of trials, not your chance. Wheat on part depends on the corn price: "Try it on a strip here" at a low price, "Tied" at the base price (4 bags/ha, 5 of 10) and "Keep what you do" at a high price (12 bags/ha, 0 of 10). "Take this to my agronomist" prints a sheet, in Portuguese and English, with a test in paired, repeated strips.

NASA data on the page

NASA HLS-VI v2.0 (Landsat and Sentinel-2, 30 m) fills an 8-season ribbon for each field, with the Zarc risk band, and places the end of the first green cycle against the Zarc corn window. It ended before the window closed in every clean season: 4 of 4 on Field A, 3 of 3 on Field B, 6 of 6 on Field C.

NASA POWER (1984 to 2025) counts cold nights and rain while each crop occupies the field. Second-crop corn: a night below 2 °C in 12 of 42 seasons, rain median 441 mm. These counts are regional.

The NASA switch turns HLS off: 0 of 18 field and option states change. So HLS is context only for the answer. It shows that the corn window is not the limit here, and when each field had no green.

Exploratory trial check

The check, fixed in PROTOCOL.md: soybean after wheat minus soybean after second-crop corn, simulated by AquaCrop-OSPy 3.1.0 (water only, never fitted to yield) against observed, in 10 trial site-seasons from 3 sites.

Result: Model not validated here. Site-seasons completed: 10 of 10. T0 (control) fail, Kendall S = 0. T1 (primary) fail, S = 11 (a pass needs 21), RMSE 896 kg/ha against 280 kg/ha for the constant. P1 fail. A1 fail. L0, run after the freeze on the three product fields, fails on 50 unexplained artifacts. The crop model stays out of the answer.

After the freeze, one sensitivity run repeated the check with the SoilGrids textures set aside before the protocol tag, because the engine's texture formula gives these very clayey soils about half the available water. The positive control then passes (S 23), but the primary contrast still fails (S 19, RMSE 1,648 kg/ha against 280 for a constant), so the label stays as frozen.

The check is exploratory and not blind. A fail means not shown, never refuted.

What it does not know

Not visible from orbit: roots, nitrogen, nematodes, disease and yield.

No forecast for next season, and no chance that an option works on a given field.

NDVI cannot separate straw from bare soil and never gives the sowing date. A date declared by the farmer rules over it.

The soil comes from SoilGrids, an estimate that never decides. The trials sit on clay above 750 g/kg under no-till.

No real farmer has used the tool. No local agronomist review was attempted. The planned comprehension test (H1) did not run.

The path to other regions

A region gets a verdict only with its own Regional Pack, with public replicated trials and a local reviewer. No field trials, no verdict. The rule travels. The verdict does not.

The data adapters and decision-rule framework are designed to be reusable across regions, but each new region requires its own evidence and validation. A new region needs its own pack, trials and protocol, or a network of on-farm trials (Lacoste et al. 2022, Nature Food). The observation page shows the first step: one field in the Free State, South Africa, read by the same end-of-green rule with NASA HLS, NASADEM and NASA POWER, and no verdict.

Tools

Python for the data pipeline and the crop model (AquaCrop-OSPy, rasterio, pandas), and a static HTML and JavaScript page (Alpine.js) with no server and no account, published with GitHub Pages. Tests in pytest and Node.
